items.quote: CHAP. II. Where that True Physick is to be Found.
items.note: The chapter is headed and numbered as the place where the True Physick is to be found.

items.quote: EVery thing that God created Good is extreamly perfect and incorruptible, as the heaven
items.note: Croll holds that what God created good is perfect and incorruptible; the heaven is his example.

items.quote: hath a twofold Nature
items.note: Sublunary things have a twofold nature, which the text then spells out as perfect and imperfect.

items.quote: a perfect and an imperfect, that is, a fift Essence and the dreggs may be separated one from the other by fire
items.note: The text says what the two natures are: the perfect is a fift Essence, the imperfect the dreggs; fire separates them.

items.quote: may be separated one from the other by fire
items.note: Step of work: the fift Essence and the dreggs are separated from each other by fire.

items.quote: the true medicine (or Physick) is wrapt up in rindes, barks, matrixes, receptacles, husks, garment and cottages
items.note: The true medicine is said to be covered by outer layers, likened to the bark and rind over kernels.

items.quote: the same must be seperated from the impure Elements by the artificiall Anotomy of Chymists before we can come at the pure Medicine
items.note: Step of work: the medicine is separated from the impure Elements by the Chymists' artificiall Anotomy to reach the pure Medicine.

items.quote: For the bonds are loosed by art and industry, and the faculties of healing set at liberty.
items.note: What the separation does: art loosens bonds and sets the healing faculties free.

items.quote: Wheat doth norgrow without a place, nor can we have meale without bran, neither is hony without a sting.
items.note: Margin examples of a good thing that comes with a husk or sting, beside the twofold nature passage.

items.quote: Such Secrets are regenerated without any complexion of qualities.
items.note: The margin calls these things Secrets and says they are regenerated without the qualities; the word Secrets points to a hidden sense.

items.quote: those three Families of Nature, the Vegetable, Animall, and Minerall
items.note: The text names three families of nature as the sources of medicines.

items.quote: there is contained that True and specifix Physick of materiall distempers
items.note: Croll holds that the True Physick is contained in all three families.

items.quote: which as hath been said, doth not consist in the four outward, naked, superficiary and Relollaceous qualities
items.note: Points back to an earlier statement that the True Physick does not lie in the four outward qualities.

items.quote: as Theophrastus learnedly discourseth
items.name: Theophrastus
items.note: Theophrastus is cited as discoursing that the physick does not lie in the outward qualities.

items.quote: it is a certaine specifix vertue concealed in the very Seeds, naturally proceeding without art
items.note: The true physick is a virtue said to be concealed in the seeds.

items.quote: which the Creator, that great Workmaster of all things, in the beginning of all the Creation planted in every growing thing by vertue of that omnipotent Word
items.note: Croll holds the hidden virtue was planted by the Creator at the beginning, through the omnipotent Word.

items.quote: The faculties and vertue therefore wherewith mixt bodies are indued (like the soule in mans body from the beginning of the Creation) is not from without
items.note: Croll holds the virtue of mixt bodies is inborn from creation, not from without.

items.quote: nor infused into them by a momomentaneous position of the Stars, nor made up of a fortuitous meeting of Atomes
items.note: Croll rejects two sources of the virtue: a momentary position of the stars, and a chance meeting of atoms.

items.quote: for then it could not be separated without the destruction and corruption of the body and forme, as we see in Cinamon and Pepper
items.note: His proof that the virtue is not from the body: it can be separated from cinnamon and pepper without destroying them.

items.quote: in which the mecanick sciences of the Three principles have their vigour
items.note: The Three principles are named as one set whose sciences have their vigour in spirits and tinctures.

items.quote: so the actions of Cures proceed from the Spirits and vitall Tinctures of the spirits, not from the bodies or dead Relloceous qualities
items.note: Croll holds cures come from spirits and vital tinctures, not from bodies or the dead qualities.

items.quote: Heaven is the framer of the externall edifices, not of the Secrets, Wonders and mysteries that dwell in them.
items.note: Margin: heaven frames only the outer buildings, not the secrets that dwell in them.

items.quote: have their force by subministration from the Heaven, and the Heaven from the Intelligences
items.note: Here inferior things have their force from the Heaven; CH2.3 says their virtue is not from without nor from the stars, and N133 that heaven frames only the outer edifices.

items.quote: it is granted by the Interpreters of Secret Nature
items.name: Interpreters of Secret Nature
items.note: A group is cited as granting that all of the Universe is in man.

items.quote: there is nothing in the whole Universe, every particular whereof is not also in that Microcosm Man, as hath been said
items.note: Man as Microcosm holds every particular of the Universe; marked as said before.

items.quote: the seeds of all things lye hid in him
items.note: The seeds of all things are said to lie hidden in man.

items.quote: this Symmetricall concord and Physicall anagoge
items.note: The correspondence between man and the world is named as one thing.

items.quote: it hath been the part of True Physitians to enquire, that if the internall Heart of the Microcosm or Man should be sick, how they might borrow strengthning remedies from his Parent
items.note: True physicians cure man's inner heart with remedies borrowed from his Parent, the outer world.

items.quote: the externall Heart of the Microcosm which is one like the other
items.note: The outer heart is called that of the Microcosm, the same name as man's; CH2.7 calls the outer counterpart Macrocosmicall.

items.quote: which remedies are analogically represented
items.note: The remedies are said to be represented by analogy, pointing to a second, correspondent sense.

items.quote: those three shops of Cures
items.note: The three sources of remedies are named as shops.

items.quote: All the whole inferiour Nature is divided into three principall parts, i. e. Vegetable, Animall, and Minerall.
items.note: Margin names the three parts that the three shops refer to.

items.quote: For God created an inexhaustible supply of medicines, and distributed to every Country sufficient for it selfe.
items.note: Croll holds God gave each country enough medicines.

items.quote: Gold (which cheareth up the Spirits when a man hath enough of it in his purse)
items.note: Gold as medicine is set beside gold as money in a purse; the word Spirits carries two senses here.

items.quote: which are produced out of the Element of Water, as Gemms and precious stones in shells are generated of drops of water
items.note: Croll holds such minerals come from the Element of Water.

items.quote: which by a specifick and Harmonicall vertue serve to cure and comfort the heart
items.note: These minerals and shellfish cure the heart by a specific, harmonical virtue.

items.quote: which sage Antiquity hath without rashnesse or superstition attributed to them
items.name: sage Antiquity
items.note: The magical characters of minerals are attributed to them by sage Antiquity.

items.quote: that doe sufficiently insinuate to Inlightned men, and Magically disclose their hidden vertue to those more secret Phylosophers that are instructed therein
items.note: The Characters disclose the hidden virtue only to enlightened, instructed philosophers.

items.quote: by Natures just decree, with-hold their benigne and vitall Element from those that possesse them
items.note: The choicest things withhold their vital Element from those who merely possess them.

items.quote: As he that hath much Gold may know nothing of its medicinall vertue.
items.note: Margin: having gold is not knowing its medicinal virtue; a second sense of possessing.

items.quote: many there are who confound the Universall Lawes of Nature, and yet thinks to partake of her Banquet in the end
items.note: Croll charges many with confounding Nature's laws while hoping for her rewards.

items.quote: the Gold would discover most Divine actions if it were rightly refined, and had its power reduced into act by a Naturall and due Resolution
items.note: Step of work: gold rightly refined and resolved has its power brought into act.

items.quote: for there is but one way to Resolve and to compound things, because Art and Nature, like mother and daughter, consent to each other
items.note: Croll holds there is one way of resolving and compounding, since Art and Nature agree.

items.quote: Art imitateth Nature and supplyeth its defects; it correcteth, chastiseth, assisteth and promoteth, yea it exceedeth Nature.
items.note: Margin: art imitates and even exceeds nature.

items.quote: but few men have this gift of God bestowed on them, so as to make solid and massy Gold potable, that it may be drunk
items.note: Making gold drinkable is a gift of God given to few.

items.quote: Amongst Vegetables there is Saffron, Rue, Balme, Scordium, Celandine, Mace, Ocymum, with six hundred of the like.
items.note: Lists vegetable medicines under the vegetable family.

items.quote: Amongst Animalls there is Hart's horn, Unicorns horn, the Bone in Staggs hearts
items.note: Lists animal medicines under the animal family.

items.quote: All which being rightly prepared in due manner, doe cure the diseases of the Heart
items.note: These remedies cure the heart only when rightly prepared.

items.quote: not (as I have said) by their Externall superficiary qualities, but by an Internall, proper, specifick, harmonious, similer virtue
items.note: Points back to his earlier statement that cure is by inner, not outer, qualities.

items.quote: for all things whatsoever serve to our health, are all contained in the Spirits, which onely know how and where to find out the disease
items.note: Croll holds all that serves health is in the Spirits, which find the disease.

items.quote: the earthy part is altogether dead, husks and rinds beget nothing, the Spirits onely in the bodies of things doe all
items.note: The earthy part and husks are dead; only spirits act.

items.quote: The Formes in thee medicines or Astra's of the medicaments separated by Alchymie from their bodies are the true Directoryes
items.note: The Formes are glossed as Astra's; separated by Alchymie they direct the cure.

items.quote: not the body, but the Astrum or hidden Heaven gives all the direction
items.note: Astrum is glossed as hidden Heaven, the director of the cure.

items.quote: every medicine striveth to get to its place, and seeketh after that member that is like unto it
items.note: Each medicine seeks the bodily member like it.

items.quote: magnetick vertue which may well be called the inexpressible property
items.note: The magnetic virtue by which like seeks like is named the inexpressible property.

items.quote: as the true Phylosophicall Phisitians have diligently observed by long Experience the most undouted Rule of all
items.name: Phylosophicall Phisitians
items.note: The rule of like to like is credited to the observation of philosophical physicians.

items.quote: Wherefore Celsus the Roman Physitian confesseth of all Arts
items.name: Celsus
items.note: Celsus is cited as confessing something of all arts.

items.quote: where by many good old country women have gone beyond great learned Physitians
items.note: Country women have surpassed learned physicians by this way of experience.

items.quote: Experiment, as also judgement, without knowledge is but fallacious difficult and fortuitous, but with Science it is true and infallible.
items.note: Margin says experiment without knowledge is fallacious, beside the text praising country women who outdo learned physicians.

items.quote: The same may be sayd of the other six principall members and parts of mans body
items.note: The body's principal members are counted as six besides the heart.

items.quote: The external Macrocosmicall Braine is the Oyle of Silver, Water of the Sophire Emerold, Mosse, Vitrioll
items.note: The text names what the outer brain of the great world is.

items.quote: The flower or CHIBUR or Brimstone are a Balsam for the lungs and the whole breast.
items.note: CHIBUR is set equal to the flower or Brimstone, a balsam for the lungs.

items.quote: After this manner not only ordinary diseases are cured by every Dunce, but also those Chronicall, Astrall and fixed diseases
items.note: By this method even chronic and astral diseases are curable.

items.quote: the common sort of Physitians who know not the seat, seeds, nativities, roots, and centres of diseases judge to be incurable
items.name: the common sort of Physitians
items.note: Common physicians judge such diseases incurable; Croll reports this to reject it.

items.quote: For there is no disease, as it is a disease, but there is a medicine for it
items.note: Croll holds every disease has a medicine.

items.quote: unlesse such as prodeth onely from the anger of the Divine Majesty by secret predestination, which cannot be found out by man
items.note: Exception: diseases from God's anger by secret predestination are hidden from man.

items.quote: the cure whereof was never given to Physitians, but to the Apostles, who by true faith in Christ healed all Diseases
items.note: Such diseases were curable only by the Apostles through faith.

items.quote: unlesse with Pliny we should belye Nature in its perfections as an unjust Step-mother
items.name: Pliny
items.note: Pliny's view of Nature as stepmother is reported to be rejected.

items.quote: provident and wise Nature hath by naturall instinct bestowed upon poor bruite creatures the knowledge of their Remedies
items.note: Nature gave animals knowledge of their remedies by instinct.

items.quote: It were therefore great folly and sottishnesse to think that the great Creator would hide these things from men
items.note: Croll holds God would not hide remedies from men.

items.quote: the great Creator would hide these things from men
items.note: Here God would not hide remedies from men; CH2.5 says the choicest things withhold their vital Element and few have the gift of potable gold.

items.quote: There is no cause to complaine of the want of medicines but onely of our ignorance of them.
items.note: Margin: lack is in our knowledge, not in medicines.

items.quote: There are two sorts of Physitians, one cure miraculously, the other naturally by means.
items.note: Margin divides physicians into miraculous and natural.

items.quote: So there are two originalls of every disease, the one naturall, the other caelestiall
items.note: Margin names two origins of disease, each with its own cure.

items.quote: Every Creature knoweth his proper remedy.
items.note: Margin summary of the animal examples.

items.quote: The Toad when stung or poysoned with any other venomous creature, eateth Rue, Sage or Plantin, or rubs the wounded part therewith and is recovered
items.note: Example of an animal cure: eating or rubbing on herbs.

items.quote: therefore it is not good to eat Sage before it be washed
items.note: A practical rule drawn from the toad's use of sage.

items.quote: And other living creatures have found out other innumerable Hearbs.
items.note: The list of animal remedies is said to go on without end.

items.quote: would in this particular neglect his own children, which he created after his own Image, and prefer the Beasts before them
items.note: No sane man will think God serves beasts better than men.

items.quote: how much rather will he subject the whole Creature, both things visible and invisible?
items.note: God, who gave his Son, will subject all creation, visible and invisible, to men.

items.quote: The most High Author of Nature ath created Medicines out of the Earth
items.note: God created medicines from the earth.

items.quote: Eccl. 38.
items.name: Eccl.
items.note: Margin cites a writing beside the passage on medicines created from the earth.

items.quote: he hath commanded the Physitians to search them out and seasonably administer them to every distemper being by due faith prepared and made up
items.note: Physicians are commanded to find and give medicines, prepared with faith.

items.quote: all medicines which are appled to mans body become efficacious and obtaine their wholesome effect, not of it selfe, but by the gift of God
items.note: Medicines work only by God's gift.

items.quote: For unlesse God be present and infuse virtue into the Hearbs what good can Dittany doe
items.note: Here God infuses virtue into herbs; CH2.3 says the virtue is not from without nor infused, and CH2.2 that it was planted in the beginning.

items.quote: For the Elements live by the Firmament, the Firmament from the Intelligible World, and this onely in God, or his Eternall Word
items.note: A chain of life from God down through the Intelligible World and Firmament to the Elements.

items.quote: and the onely life of all, and in all, yet variously sprouting forth according to the subject into which it flows
items.note: God is the one life, appearing differently in each subject.

items.quote: In all the things of the God of Nature, not Nature but
items.note: Margin: in natural things the Lord's will, not Nature, is to be implored.

items.quote: if we intend to doe any good with hearbs, we must not trust so much to them as to God
items.note: Trust belongs to God more than to herbs.

items.quote: Asa dyed because he trusted more to the Physitians then to God.
items.name: Asa
items.note: Asa is given as an example of one who died trusting physicians over God.

items.name: 2 Chro.
items.note: Margin cites the writing behind the Asa example.

items.quote: The Caelestiall Medicine onely, or the WORD of God
items.note: The Caelestiall Medicine is said to be the WORD of God.

items.quote: which is the Firmament of all Physick
items.note: The Word is called the Firmament of all Physick, a use of Firmament other than the heaven of CH2.12.

items.quote: in which lyeth hid, and from which proceedeth all force beyond any naturall actions
items.note: All force is said to lie hidden in the Word.

items.name: Psal.; Eccl.
items.note: Margin cites writings beside the passage on the Word as medicine.

items.quote: As the bark is not the kernell, so hearbs are not the medicines, but a signe onely of the Word signified.
items.note: Herbs are said to be only a sign of the Word; the bark and kernel figure of CH2.1 now points to the Word.

items.quote: the Hearb is not the medicine, for that is invisibly hid in God himselfe
items.note: Here the medicine is hid in God, not in the herb; CH2.1 has the true medicine in the kernel of things, reached by the Chymists' separation.

items.quote: Physick is two-fold in the Earth, Visible, which the Father hath created
items.note: Physick is divided into two: Visible from the Father, and Invisible from the Son.

items.quote: ought not to be administred before there be a separation of the pure from the impure
items.note: Visible physick must be separated, pure from impure, before it is given.

items.quote: Invisible, from the Son by the Word, and is but one
items.note: The second physick is invisible, one, and from the Son by the Word.

items.quote: Almighty God could (and can) make men whole by the Prophets and True Cabalists with a word onely
items.note: God heals by a word through Prophets and True Cabalists.

items.quote: Acts 3.6.
items.name: Acts
items.note: Margin cites a writing beside healing by a word.

items.quote: God is a living God, the NAME also of the living God is lively, and so the Letters of the living Name are also lively
items.note: Life passes from God to his Name and from the Name to its Letters.

items.quote: True Magicians (by whom I doe not mean Nicromancers or them of the Black Art) those accurate searchers out of Nature
items.note: True Magicians are defined as searchers of Nature, not necromancers.

items.quote: framed at a certaine time according to the power of Heaven, far from all superstition
items.note: Characters or Signes are made at a set time according to the power of Heaven.

items.quote: otherwise it were better for us alwayes to be sick then to be cured with the dishonour of God
items.note: Croll would rather stay sick than be cured dishonourably to God.

items.quote: For Characters or constellated Names according to Agrippa, have no force from the Figureors Pronunciation
items.name: Agrippa
items.note: Agrippa is cited: characters have no force from their shape or sound but from the office God or Nature gave them.

items.quote: Such Names are the Divine Power.
items.note: Margin says what such Names are.

items.quote: There is no vertue or power either in Heaven or Earth which descendeth not from God
items.note: All power descends from God.

items.quote: Medicines are visible bodies; Words are invisible bodies
items.note: Medicines and words are set side by side as visible and invisible bodies.

items.quote: by the Spirit of God made One with Nature by his Word FIAT
items.note: Healing by herb or word is by God's Spirit joined to Nature through the Word FIAT.

items.quote: Concerning Characteristicalll Cure which affecteth Naturall operations by words pronounced, written, carved and hanged about the neck
items.note: A kind of cure by words and characters is named.

items.quote: let him read Rog. Bacon of the wonderfull power of Art and Nature
items.name: Rog. Bacon
items.note: Readers are sent to Rog. Bacon for characteristical cure.

items.quote: Paracels. saith that Characters are
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: Margin gives Paracels. a statement about Characters; part of it is illegible.

items.quote: Physitians also have wrought great cures by the Created Word, or the incarnate Mercy
items.note: Physicians have cured by the Word called Created and incarnate Mercy.

items.quote: he did it by One Word, and he is that Word, to wit, the increated Mercy of God
items.note: The Saviour is the Word, glossed as the increated Mercy; the same paragraph earlier says Created Word.

items.quote: to whom the Pills and Syrups of all the Shops in the world could doe no good
items.note: No apothecary's remedy could help those the Saviour healed.

items.quote: Luke 11.14.
items.name: Luke
items.note: Margin cites a writing beside the Saviour's miracles.

items.quote: Grace exceedeth Nature, and the thing signified excelleth the signe.
items.note: Margin: grace exceeds nature, the thing signified the sign.

items.quote: John 1.3. Not by bread alone, Mat. 4.4.
items.name: John; Mat.
items.note: Margin cites writings beside the Word by which all things are made.

items.quote: which Spirit therefore is the only fulnes of the whole world
items.note: The one Spirit filling all things is the fulness of the world, and is named The Fulnesse.

items.quote: and may well be called The Fulnesse.
items.note: The Spirit is given a name of its own.

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: Margin cites a writing beside The Fulnesse.

items.quote: Nothing is made out of God, for in him all things live, are moved and doe subsist.
items.note: All things live and subsist in God.

items.quote: This WORD of God, the First begotten of every Creature, is truly our Dayly Bread
items.note: The Word is said to be the daily bread prayed for.

items.quote: it is the supercaelestiall Mummy, the supernaturall Balsome comforting poor Mortalls more then Mans own Mummy or naturall Balsom
items.note: The Word is called a supercelestial Mummy and Balsome, above man's natural Mummy.

items.quote: The vertue in bread is the blessing of God, yea God himselfe
items.note: The virtue in bread is said to be God's blessing, God himself.

items.quote: Man liveth not by bread alone, but by that which is in Bread
items.note: Life comes from what is in bread, the Word.

items.quote: If the Word were not, or of it selfe were not the onely Bread, then the Earth would be our God
items.note: Argument: without the Word as bread, the Earth would be our God.

items.quote: It is of mere mercy and goodnesse not of justice that we have both the bread of nourishment and of healing.
items.note: Margin: food and healing come from mercy, not justice.

items.quote: Without this benediction the staffe of bread is broken, a God threatned his people by his Prophets.
items.name: his Prophets
items.note: Margin gives a threat God made through his Prophets.

items.quote: This Word then is the true medicine that healeth all things, but is not known to every one
items.note: The Word as true medicine is not known to everyone.

items.quote: nor can every Scholler treat and write of it though plunged over head and eares in the dusty learning of School-Divinity
items.note: School learning does not fit a scholar to write of the Word as medicine.

items.quote: our friend Theophrastus Paracelsus a Disciple of the Mosaicall and Living Phylosophy hath written of the Secrets of Nature and the Wonders of God
items.name: Theophrastus Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus is named as having written of the Secrets of Nature.

items.quote: to wit, of the WORD of God INCARNATE which may be found in the Creatures
items.note: The Secrets of Nature are glossed as the incarnate Word found in creatures.

items.quote: by this Word, FIAT, the seed of the whole world, were Heaven and Earth created
items.note: FIAT is called the seed of the whole world.

items.name: John; Heb.; Psal.
items.note: Margin cites writings beside the incarnate Word.

items.quote: that the MAGUS, the Wise man or Caelestiall Physitian performeth suddenly and much sooner by Characters and Stones with a most powerfull impression
items.note: MAGUS is glossed as Wise man or Caelestiall Physitian; he does quickly by characters and stones what herbs do slowly.

items.quote: to wit, the Gamahaea of Influentiall Wedlock to the Terrestiall signe, by matrimoniall combination of the Superiors and Inferiors ASTRALLY
items.note: The powerful impression is glossed as the Gamahaea, a wedding of heavenly influence to an earthly sign.

items.quote: like a stretched cord, all the Superiour vertue floweth through every inferiour thing even to the utmost
items.note: Higher virtue runs through all lower things like a stretched cord.

items.quote: the inferiour passe through all to their Superiours, because the working Vertue is one
items.note: The lower things also reach the higher, the virtue being one.

items.quote: Divine Matrimony
items.note: Marriage is used for the bond of higher and lower things, a figure the paragraph repeats (Wedlock, matrimoniall, marriage).

items.quote: many things may be done in Magick and Cabal by the intercession of the worlds marriage
items.note: Magick and Cabal work through the world's marriage.

items.quote: in Hearbs Stones and Words there are great vertues.
items.note: Margin says the paragraph explains a common saying about herbs, stones and words.

items.quote: And the True Cabalist (whom Paracelsus calls the Naturall Divine, who is equall to the Prophets
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus' name for the True Cabalist is given: the Naturall Divine.

items.quote: whose mind being united and coaequant to God doth whatsoever he will, for he willeth onely what God doth
items.note: The Cabalist's will is one with God's.

items.quote: he doth above Nature, DEALLY or like God accomplish complish in a moment by firme confidence and strong faith
items.note: DEALLY is glossed as like God; the Cabalist works above nature in a moment by faith.

items.quote: the very GATE of miracles in that Only Divine Name ISHUH in which all things are reckoned up and contained
items.note: A single divine Name is named as the gate of miracles, containing all things.

items.quote: that is he doth performe it in the WONDERFULL WORD by the Mind, Faith and Prayer, to wit, prayers made in Spirit and in Truth
items.note: The text says how the Cabalist works: by Mind, Faith and Prayer.

items.quote: The New Birth is the Field of Caelestiall Physick which healeth with a word without Externall means
items.note: The New Birth is named the field of celestial physick.

items.quote: that one operation is in respect of God as the Artificer, and in respect of Man as the Instrument
items.note: God is the worker, man the instrument.

items.quote: who are heard in all things whatsoever they pray for, witnesse Elias, Elisha
items.name: Elias, Elisha
items.note: Elias and Elisha are named as witnesses of faith that is heard.

items.quote: Every Creature feareth and reverenceth his Name that made it.
items.note: Margin: all creatures fear the Name of their maker.

items.quote: Read the books of the Kings. 1 Kings 3.12. Wifd. 7.
items.name: the books of the Kings; Wifd.
items.note: Margin sends the reader to writings beside the faithful who are heard.

items.quote: By prayer in Faith we obtaine all things, I mean (not a lazy, sluggish prayer, but) a constant asking, seeking, knocking
items.note: Croll holds that constant prayer in faith obtains all things.

items.quote: For in these Three principall Poynts also consisteth the whole Foundation of the Magicall and Cabalisticall Art
items.note: Three points (apparently Mind, Faith and Prayer, named just before) are set apart as the foundation of the magical and cabalistical art; this reading is mine.

items.quote: as appeareth by Paracelsus in his third book of the Signature of Things
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus' third book of the Signature of Things is cited for the three points.

items.quote: Honour and Praise and Glory therefore belongeth to the Creator, who worketh all in all
items.note: The credit for cure belongs to God.

items.quote: For there is nothing at all of his own in it besides Art and right preparation
items.note: The physician's own share is only art and right preparation.

items.quote: will not give his Honour to another
items.note: God keeps all honour for himself.

items.quote: We are not to ascribe our bodily health to the Physitian but to God.
items.note: Margin: health is ascribed to God, not the physician.

items.quote: but proudly and rashly promise a set and certaine time of recovery which is to be left to God onely
items.note: Margin rebukes physicians who promise a fixed time of recovery.

items.quote: the true and sincere Physitian, who among all arts and faculties is most accepted of God, is to be honoured as the Scripture commandeth
items.note: Yet the true physician is to be honoured; three reasons follow.

items.quote: First, because God worketh and doth his own will by him as by his Minister, when he sleepeth and knoweth it not
items.note: First numbered reason for honouring the physician: God works through him even unawares.

items.quote: saith our Saviour, ye can nothing
items.name: our Saviour
items.note: The Saviour's words are cited: without me ye can nothing.

items.quote: John 15.
items.name: John
items.note: Margin cites the source of the Saviour's words.

items.quote: Secondly, because (Health being the greatest Good to men) he ought to excell all mortalls in the search and knowledge of Nature and the Light thereof
items.note: Second reason: the physician must excel in knowledge of Nature and its Light.

items.quote: Not in vaine therefore did Homer require a Physitian to be furnished with all knowledge
items.name: Homer
items.note: Homer is cited as requiring all knowledge of a physician.

items.quote: Thirdly, because he alone manifesteth to all, the wonderfull works of God both in the great and little world
items.note: Third reason: the physician shows God's works in the great and little world.

items.quote: not onely by opening his mysteryes and hidden secrets, but also by curing the sick
items.note: The physician opens God's mysteries and hidden secrets.

items.quote: Physick is to be accounted the most excellent, wherein the greatest wonders of God are miraculously seen
items.note: Croll ranks physick above all sciences.

items.quote: It taketh its rise from Theology or the Light of Grace, and endeth in the Light of Nature.
items.note: Theology is glossed as the Light of Grace; physick runs from it to the Light of Nature.
